title: Exposure to (AI-Generated) Untrustworthy Websites in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
screen_reason: Digital-trace study (YouGov Pulse browsing logs, N = 1,069 US adults, ~6M visits, 8 Oct-12 Nov 2024) matched against expert domain lists of untrustworthy websites. Reports the share of Americans who visited at least one untrustworthy website (behavioural REACH), the share who visited an AI-generated untrustworthy site, the mean number of untrustworthy visits among the exposed, and the share of untrustworthy visits that were AI-generated. Multiple quantitative shares with explicit denominators.

estimates.platform: Web browsing across desktop, smartphone and tablet (YouGov Pulse passive metering)
estimates.measure_type: % of American adults who visited at least one untrustworthy website during the 2024 election period
estimates.denominator: 1,069 American adults recruited by YouGov with Pulse metering software installed (weighted to US benchmarks)
estimates.definition: At least one visit, in the URL-level browsing log, to a domain on the 2,573-domain general untrustworthy list (Grinberg et al. 490 + Allcott & Gentzkow 66 + NewsGuard 'repeatedly publishes false content' 1,240 + 777 added since 2020)
estimates.misinfo_def: Untrustworthy online content-information that contradicts the best available evidence from experts at the time
estimates.source_quote: In 2024, 16.5% (95% CI [13.7%, 19.4%]) of Americans visited at least one untrustworthy website, a significant decline from the 26.1% (95% CI [22.5%, 29.8%]) who did so in 2020 (H1, t = -5.567, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.236, one-tailed) and the 44.3% (95% CI [40.8%, 47.7%]) who did so in 2016 (see Figure 1).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Total consumption of untrustworthy websites in 2024' (p. 7); also SI S1 (H1b)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level lists compiled by third parties: 490 domains from Grinberg et al. (382 'identified by journalists and fact checkers as notable publishers of false or misleading content'), 66 from Allcott & Gentzkow, and 2,017 NewsGuard domains rated as 'repeatedly publishing false content'; no inter-coder reliability reported (external expert ratings)
estimates.moderator_quote: We matched our updated lists against each participant's URL-level browsing logs so that any visit to a domain on these lists was classified as an exposure to untrustworthy content, distinguishing between non-AI and AI-generated sites.
estimates.notes: Headline estimate of the paper's own 2024 data collection. The 2020 (26.1%) and 2016 (44.3%) figures are the authors' re-analyses of the earlier YouGov Pulse datasets from Moore et al. and Guess et al.; per the time-series rule only the 2024 point is kept here (see missed_or_uncertain). Topic coded politics_elections: the untrustworthy list is a political/hard-news domain list and the field period is the election, but the log covers all browsing.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) The 2020 and 2016 comparison figures (26.1% and 44.3% any exposure; 2.6% AI exposure in 2020; 2.1% AI share of exposures in 2020; 22.8 mean visits among exposed) are the authors' own re-analyses of the earlier YouGov Pulse waves reported by Moore et al. and Guess et al.; I collapsed the three-election series to the paper's own 2024 collection and did not create rows for the earlier waves (they belong to the earlier papers). (2) Referrer shares (Twitter/X 2.3%, Facebook 2.1%, Google 6.0%, YouTube 4.5% of visits to untrustworthy sites in 2024) are pathway composition within misinformation visits, not a prevalence of misinformation on those platforms - not extracted. (3) Further subgroup breakdowns not extracted: Trump vs Harris supporters (29.0% vs 8.9%), registered vs non-registered voters (17.6% vs 7.5%), ideology deciles (Very Conservative 33.1%, Conservative 29.0%, Moderate 9.3%, Liberal 9.6%, Very Liberal 9.9%), generational rates (Table S2: Silent 19.1%, Boomers 25.7%, Gen X 14.6%, Millennial 7.9%, Gen Z 12.8%), and AI-exposure subgroups (65+ 5.8%, 18-29 10.0%, Republicans 7.4%, Democrats 5.0%). These are one level below the headline and would multiply rows without adding an independent estimate. (4) SI S20 reports a separate Verasight survey (N = 1,000, April 2025) in which 55.6% of Americans thought untrustworthy-website exposure had increased from 2020 to 2024 - this is a perception of a national trend, not self-reported exposure or perceived amount of misinformation in one's own environment, so no RECALL row. (5) Untrustworthy visits as a share of all website visits are shown only in Figure S4 panels C/F (axis maxima 0.3% and 0.75%); the text says only that even for the Silent Generation such sites 'accounted for less than 1% of web visits', which is not a point estimate. (6) Average visit duration (53 s non-AI, 44 s AI) is not a share. (7) Self-assessed exposure (S9.1) was asked as an integer count of visits, never as a share of respondents, so no RECALL row.

rob.design: Preregistered (OSF CS3Z6) digital-trace + survey study. YouGov recruited 1,069 US adults into a two-wave survey with YouGov Pulse metering on computers, smartphones and tablets; passive URL-level logs 8 Oct-12 Nov 2024 (~6M visits); YouGov weights to US demographic benchmarks and all analyses are weighted; no response/attrition rate reported. Misinformation classified at the domain level by matching logs to expert-curated lists (2,573 general untrustworthy domains from Grinberg et al., Allcott & Gentzkow and NewsGuard; 810 NewsGuard UAINS AI-generated domains); no inter-coder reliability computed because classification is list-based. Stated limitations: domain-level classification misses within-domain variation, browser logs miss in-app and feed exposure, normality assumed but not tested.
